summary:
I've been building a Japanese-learning app for myself, and the biggest piece of it this year was a grammar engine that turned out to have no verb in it. Sentences like "eat rice" were literally stored as fixed text — the verb was baked into a template string, which meant nothing could conjugate. I rebuilt it so a verb is its own entry with a conjugation class, sourced from a real dictionary (guessing the class from spelling is wrong often enough to matter — a third of common verbs don't inflect the way their ending suggests). The payoff: a grammar rule that used to need a new hand-written template now costs a few lines of data. It's up to 26 verbs, 70 sentence patterns, and about 3,200 generated example sentences, all validated by feeding them back through a text-to-speech engine and checking it actually reads them the way a native speaker would.

That same project turned up a genuinely funny bug: a Japanese sentence I generated, "はねた" ("jumped"), gets parsed by any real reader as a totally different word — the topic marker は got swallowed into the verb and read wrong. I could've patched the pronunciation to force it, but that would've taught a reading that doesn't actually happen in real Japanese, so I left it broken and just blocked that one combination instead. Sometimes the right fix is admitting the sentence shouldn't exist.

I also chased down a mis-tap bug on the phone version that looked like a routing problem for a full day before it turned out to be pure layout: two buttons sitting 7 pixels apart, one 35 pixels tall (Apple's own minimum is 44), so a thumb aimed at one reliably landed on its neighbor and opened the wrong thing. Four layers of code were innocent; the fix was deleting the button rather than making it bigger.

On the automation side, I run a personal agent (Hermes-Agent) that handles scheduling and messages for my household, and a cron job in it once caused every conversation to silently start refusing to run code — a global flag meant to apply only during a scheduled job never got cleared, so it stuck for every session that came after. Tracked it to one process-wide variable and fixed it with a reference count instead of a boolean, so the flag can't outlive the job that set it.

highlights.oneLiner: Traced a stuck cron flag that silently disabled code execution app-wide; fixed with a refcount.
